extracted.intended_audience: writers, students, editors, and teachers seeking concise American English usage and composition guidance
extracted.subtask_description: A concise, prescriptive style guide for clear American English prose that lists rules of usage, principles of composition, matters of form, and common word-usage and spelling pitfalls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit needless words
rubrics_metrics.description: "Omit needless words." — a central injunction of Strunk & White: "Vigorous writing is concise. A sentence should contain no unnecessary words, a paragraph no unnecessary sentences..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make every word tell; concision does not require making all sentences short or avoiding necessary detail, but requires cutting unnecessary words and sentences. (Quoted in the book's "Elementary Principles of Composition".)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the active voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocate using the active voice rather than passive constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strunk urged preference for active voice to promote clarity and vigor in prose; the Wikipedia page cites this as a key early recommendation from the 1918 text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ parallelism appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Use parallel construction where appropriate to improve clarity and rhythm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parallelism is listed among Strunk's elementary recommendations for composition; use consistent grammatical forms in series, comparisons, and constructions that are meant to balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer the standard to the offbeat
rubrics_metrics.description: "Prefer the standard to the offbeat." — the 21st reminder in Chapter V: a general recommendation to favor conventional phrasing and usage over striking but nonstandard alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This admonition appears as a thematic summary of the book's preference for clarity and conventional standards of English over novelty for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write to please yourself; aim for 'one moment of felicity'
rubrics_metrics.description: E. B. White's advice that writers should have the mindset of writing to please themselves and to aim for "one moment of felicity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is prescriptive guidance about authorial attitude and stylistic goals: prioritize moments of exact phrasing and felicity rather than mechanical rule-following alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of gender-neutral pronouns / avoid generic 'he'
rubrics_metrics.description: Modernized guidance on pronouns: avoid exclusive use of "he" for generic antecedents; use alternatives such as "his or her," "you," "they," or "the writer."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The fourth edition replaces Strunk's older guidance and explicitly notes that many writers find the generic "he" limiting or offensive; choose inclusive phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elementary rules of usage (eight rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: The book comprises eight "elementary rules of usage" (original formulation); these are foundational usage prescriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Wikipedia article notes the book's structure includes these eight rules though it does not enumerate them on the page; they serve as core usage constraints for American English prose in the manual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elementary principles of composition (ten principles / 11 in later editions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of elementary principles of composition (ten in early editions; 11 principles appear in later editions) intended to guide paragraph and sentence-level composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These principles include rules such as concision, structure, emphasis, openings, and closings; Wikipedia references the general category and the book's exhortations (e.g., make every word tell).

rubrics_metrics.name: Matters of form
rubrics_metrics.description: A short section called "a few matters of form" (and later expanded to 11 matters of form) providing prescriptive formatting and presentational guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This covers conventional matters of style and presentation (chapter-level constraints and formatting norms); the Wikipedia page refers to the component without listing specific items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules of punctuation and grammar (11 rules in third edition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit, numbered rules of punctuation and grammar (the third edition contains 11 such rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are prescriptive punctuation/grammar rules intended for practical application; the Wikipedia article notes their presence and gives an example of a modernized recommendation (removal of comma in 'Strunk Jr.').

rubrics_metrics.name: Lists of commonly misused words and misspellings
rubrics_metrics.description: The work contains a list of 49 "words and expressions commonly misused" and a list of 57 "words often misspelled."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These lists function as a prescriptive reference for word choice and spelling; the Wikipedia page records the counts and the inclusion of these lists as a major component of the manual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid split infinitives (prescriptive admonition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Strunk & White proscribe split infinitives (one of their prescriptive 'pet peeves').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Wikipedia article notes this as an example of the book's prescriptivism and also records scholarly criticism that such proscription is misguided — i.e., the rule is prescriptive and controversial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict use of 'which' in restrictive relative clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: The authors discourage using "which" in restrictive relative clauses (preferring "that"), another prescriptive usage rule criticized by linguists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page records that critics (e.g., Geoffrey Pullum) argue the book's proscription of this usage is incorrect; nevertheless it has been presented historically as a rule in the manual.

rubrics_metrics.name: General prescriptivist approach to clarity, accuracy, and brevity
rubrics_metrics.description: An overarching standard: promote cleanliness, accuracy, and brevity in English prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterizes Strunk's aim (quoted as a "forty-three-page summation of the case for cleanliness, accuracy, and brevity in the use of English"); this frames the other, specific rules as serving those ends.
